body.text: The Agentic Shift in Scientific Workflows

OpenAI has recently outlined a vision where agentic AI systems will fundamentally reshape scientific computing. Rather than serving as passive text generators, these agents are expected to orchestrate complex workflows: they can parse literature, formulate hypotheses, design experiments, and then execute the necessary computational steps autonomously. This represents a paradigm shift from the traditional human-in-the-loop model, where researchers manually iterate between data collection and analysis, to a system where the AI itself drives the discovery pipeline.

The implications for inference economics are profound. In the current era, running large language models is expensive, often dominated by the cost of generating tokens. However, as agentic systems become more prevalent, the architecture of these applications will likely change. We may see a move toward smaller, highly specialized models that handle specific sub-tasks within a larger agent graph, reducing the overall compute burden. This mirrors strategies already adopted in other domains: instead of deploying one massive model for every query, enterprises are beginning to consider modular stacks where a lightweight orchestrator coordinates several niche experts.

body.text: Where LLMs Fail: The Rise of Large Tabular Models

A critical boundary for current generative AI is structured data. While LLMs excel at unstructured text, they struggle with the precision required in financial reporting, scientific datasets, and tabular records. IEEE Spectrum highlights that large tabular models are emerging to fill this gap, excelling where LLMs fail. These systems are trained specifically on numerical grids and relational databases, learning patterns of correlation and causality that differ fundamentally from the linguistic patterns LLMs ingest.

For financial analysts, this distinction is vital. The shift toward tabular models suggests a new layer in the AI stack dedicated to data integrity and auditability. Unlike the probabilistic nature of text generation, which can hallucinate numbers, tabular models aim for deterministic or near-deterministic outputs, provided they are trained on high-quality datasets. This creates a bifurcated inference economy: one stream optimized for creative reasoning and another for rigorous calculation.

body.text: Data Boundaries and the Labor of Training

The sources of training data are evolving alongside the models themselves. Wired recounts an experiment where a private chef filmed a meal preparation to generate robot training data. While this sounds like a novelty, it underscores a broader trend: the labor involved in curating high-fidelity datasets is becoming a distinct, and perhaps outsourced, component of AI development. Whether it is human experts annotating code for agentic systems or robots capturing physical interactions, the cost of data creation is rising.

This raises questions about data boundaries. As models grow more sophisticated, the marginal utility of additional public web data diminishes. Organizations will increasingly rely on proprietary, internal datasets to fine-tune their systems. For a company like NTT DATA, which has integrated Codex to reduce incident analysis time to 30 minutes, this means leveraging internal operational logs rather than generic internet text. The competitive advantage will shift from access to broad public data toward the quality and exclusivity of private data silos.
The Chip Talent Battle and Deflating Hype

Technology Review reports on a fierce battle for chip talent, noting that the initial hype around AI has begun to deflate. The supply of advanced silicon remains constrained, while demand from every sector—from healthcare to finance—continues to surge. This imbalance forces companies to rethink their product strategies. Rather than chasing the latest model architecture, firms must optimize inference efficiency and perhaps accept slower training cycles in exchange for hardware availability.

The operational consequences are already visible. Teams are restructuring around hybrid work models to attract top talent, but the core challenge remains physical: the availability of GPUs and specialized accelerators. In an agentic future, where systems might run continuously in the background, hardware constraints will dictate not just model size, but system uptime and reliability. Safety and security protocols will also tighten, as the stakes for autonomous decision-making increase.
Product Strategy in a Constrained Environment

Given these constraints, product strategy must pivot. The era of simply scaling up model parameters is giving way to an era of scaling down and specializing. We are likely to see products that combine a small, efficient tabular model with a larger, more general-purpose LLM, orchestrated by a lightweight agent. This hybrid approach allows organizations to leverage the best of both worlds: the precision of structured data handling and the reasoning capabilities of generative models, all while managing inference costs effectively.

items: Prioritize modular architectures that separate reasoning from calculation.
Invest in proprietary data pipelines to reduce reliance on public datasets.
Design systems with built-in safety checks, acknowledging that autonomous agents will operate at scale.
Optimize for latency and throughput rather than raw model size.

body.text: Labor design will also require adaptation. If data curation is becoming a specialized task, companies may need to create new roles focused on dataset engineering alongside traditional software development. The integration of Codex by NTT DATA demonstrates that even routine incident analysis can be accelerated by AI, freeing up human engineers for higher-value problem solving. However, this transition is not without friction; the cultural shift from manual verification to trusting automated outputs requires significant training and process overhaul.

As we look toward the next few years, the narrative of AI as a monolithic breakthrough is giving way to a more nuanced reality. We are entering an era where the infrastructure—chips, data, and specialized models—is just as critical as the algorithms themselves. The agentic systems that promise to revolutionize scientific computing will only succeed if they navigate these constraints intelligently.

The landscape is moving fast, but the fundamentals of economics and engineering remain steady. Companies that recognize the shift from text generation to structured reasoning, and that prepare for a hardware-constrained future, will find themselves ahead of the curve. Those that continue to chase hype without addressing the underlying bottlenecks risk falling behind as the market matures.
What changes in practice

For AI, the operational question is whether the news changes how products are built, deployed, governed, or paid for. A model announcement matters most when it shifts inference cost, reliability, data boundaries, security exposure, or the amount of work a team can safely delegate to automation.

Second-order effects

The second-order question is trust. Teams do not adopt artificial intelligence because a demo is impressive; they adopt it when the workflow is observable, the failure mode is bounded, and the economics still make sense after compliance, support, latency, and human review are counted.

Leo's operating lens is to look for the control point. Sometimes it is the model, sometimes the distribution channel, sometimes the data contract, and sometimes the boring integration layer that decides whether a capability becomes a dependable product.
What to watch next

The next useful check is adoption quality. Pilots, demos, and benchmark claims are weaker signals than durable workflows, clear ownership, measured costs, and evidence that customers trust the system enough to use it in consequential work.

The practical discipline is to avoid treating the freshest headline as the whole story. The stronger read is slower and more mechanical: identify the constraint, watch whether it spreads, and keep revising the map as better evidence arrives.
